title: Deductible vs. Out-of-Pocket Maximum: What's the Difference?
summary: Deductible vs out of pocket maximum: what each one means, what counts toward them, 2026 federal limits, and how to use both when comparing health plans.
body_markdown:
Your health insurance deductible is the amount you pay for covered care before your plan starts sharing costs. Your out-of-pocket maximum is the most you'll pay for covered in-network care in a plan year. These two numbers shape every dollar you spend on medical care, and understanding the difference is one of the most useful things you can do before choosing a health plan during open enrollment.


**The short answer:** The deductible controls what you pay first; the out-of-pocket maximum controls the most you'll ever pay. Every deductible dollar counts toward your out-of-pocket max, but the max also includes copayments and coinsurance. If you're generally healthy, you'll feel the deductible more. If you face a serious medical event, the out-of-pocket maximum is your financial safety net. Knowing both, and how they interact, helps you pick the right insurance plan and decide how much to set aside in an HSA or FSA.


## What Is a Health Insurance Deductible?


A deductible is the fixed dollar amount you pay out of pocket for covered health care services each plan year before your insurer starts sharing costs. For a fuller walkthrough, see our guide to[what a deductible is and how it works](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-is-a-deductible) . The key points:


- **You pay first.** Until you reach the deductible, you pay the full negotiated rate your in-network providers charge for covered services like lab tests, imaging, specialist visits, and prescriptions.
- **Deductibles are separate from monthly premiums.** Your premium keeps your coverage active; it does not count toward your deductible or your out-of-pocket maximum.
- **Deductibles reset annually.** Both the deductible and the out-of-pocket maximum reset to zero at the start of each plan year, typically January 1 for calendar-year plans, though some employer plans use a different cycle.
- **Some plans have more than one deductible.** Many health plans carry a single medical deductible, but others add a separate prescription drug deductible or a separate deductible for out-of-network care.
- **Preventive care is usually covered before the deductible.** Under the[Affordable Care Act](https://www.healthcare.gov/choose-a-plan/your-total-costs/) , most plans cover preventive services like annual checkups, vaccinations, and screenings at $0, even if you haven't paid anything toward your deductible.
- **Deductibles vary widely by plan.** Low-deductible plans often have higher monthly premiums, sometimes with deductibles under $1,000. High-deductible health plans (HDHPs) that qualify for an HSA must have a deductible of at least $1,700 for self-only coverage and $3,400 for family coverage in 2026. Among workers with employer coverage and a general deductible, the average single deductible was[$1,886 in 2025, according to KFF](https://www.kff.org/health-costs/2025-employer-health-benefits-survey/) .


## What Is an Out-of-Pocket Maximum?


The out-of-pocket maximum (sometimes called the out-of-pocket limit) is the most you'll pay in a plan year for covered health care services through your deductible, copays, and coinsurance combined. It's the ceiling on your financial exposure for in-network care.


- **It caps your annual spending on covered care.** Once you reach it, your plan pays 100% of covered in-network services for the rest of the plan year.
- **Premiums don't count toward it.** Neither do charges for services your plan doesn't cover or, on most plans, out-of-network care. Generally, only your share of covered, in-network costs counts toward the out-of-pocket maximum.
- **It includes your deductible, copayments, and coinsurance.** Every dollar you pay toward those for covered in-network care moves you closer to the cap.
- **Federal law sets a hard cap.** For 2026, the[out-of-pocket maximum on Marketplace and other non-grandfathered plans](https://www.healthcare.gov/glossary/out-of-pocket-maximum-limit/) can be no more than **$10,600** for an individual and **$21,200** for a family. Healthcare.gov lists the 2027 limits as $12,000 and $24,000. HSA-qualified HDHPs have a lower ceiling: $8,500 self-only and $17,000 family in 2026.
- **Out-of-network care is often handled separately.** Many plans set a separate, higher limit for out-of-network care, or don't cap those costs at all.
- **It resets each plan year** , just like the deductible.


## Deductible vs. Out-of-Pocket Maximum at a Glance


Here's a side-by-side view of the two most important cost limits in your health plan:


**Factor**


**Deductible**


**Out-of-pocket maximum**


**What it is**


The amount you pay for covered care before insurance begins sharing costs


The most you'll pay in a plan year for covered in-network care


**What counts toward it**


Payments for covered health care services (not premiums or non-covered services)


Deductible payments, copays, and coinsurance for covered in-network services


**When you typically reach it**


Early in the year if you use medical services regularly


Usually only in years with major medical costs, like surgery or a hospital stay


**What happens after you reach it**


Cost sharing begins: you pay copays or coinsurance and your plan pays the rest


Your plan pays 100% of covered in-network care for the rest of the plan year


**2026 federal limits**


HSA-qualified HDHPs: at least $1,700 self-only / $3,400 family


No more than $10,600 individual / $21,200 family ($8,500 / $17,000 for HDHPs)


**Relationship**


Part of the out-of-pocket maximum


Includes the deductible plus all other in-network cost sharing


The deductible determines what you pay first. The out-of-pocket maximum protects you from a worst-case year. They aren't separate costs stacked on top of each other: every dollar you pay toward your deductible also counts toward your out-of-pocket max.


## Which Matters More for Your Monthly Budget?


Most people choosing a health insurance plan during open enrollment think first about what it will cost each month. That's where the trade-off between your deductible and your monthly premium takes center stage.


Higher premiums usually come with lower deductibles. If you rarely visit the doctor beyond preventive care, those extra premium dollars may never come back to you: you'd pay more every month for a lower threshold you never reach. Consider two plans:


- **Plan A:** $1,000 deductible, $5,000 out-of-pocket max, higher monthly premiums
- **Plan B:** $3,000 deductible, $7,000 out-of-pocket max, lower monthly premiums


In a light year, Plan B likely costs less overall because you pay less in premiums and may never reach either deductible. In a heavy year, Plan A's lower out-of-pocket maximum could leave you paying less in total, even after the higher premiums. To compare, add up a year of premiums and the out-of-pocket maximum for each plan; that's your worst-case cost.


For someone in good health who wants to keep monthly costs down, the deductible is the number you'll feel most, because it's the first threshold you hit when you need covered care. But ignoring the out-of-pocket maximum can be costly if you develop a chronic condition or face an unexpected surgery.


## Which Protects You in a Worst-Case Year?


A worst-case year means a major surgery, a complicated pregnancy, a cancer diagnosis, or a serious accident: the kind of event that generates tens of thousands of dollars in medical bills. This is where the out-of-pocket maximum becomes the most important number on your plan.


Imagine a $25,000 covered surgery on a plan with a $2,000 deductible, 20% coinsurance, and a $6,000 out-of-pocket maximum:


1. **You pay the first $2,000** (your deductible).
2. **You pay 20% coinsurance on the remaining $23,000,** which would be $4,600, bringing your total to $6,600.
3. **The out-of-pocket maximum stops you at $6,000.** You pay $4,000 in coinsurance instead of $4,600, and your plan pays 100% of covered in-network care for the rest of the plan year.


On bigger bills, the gap grows. Without a cap, 20% coinsurance on a $150,000 hospitalization would be $29,600 after the deductible. With a $6,000 out-of-pocket maximum, your share stays at $6,000.


For families, federal rules add another layer of protection: on non-grandfathered plans, no single person can be required to pay more than the individual cap ($10,600 in 2026), even if the plan has a higher family limit.


The trade-off: plans with lower out-of-pocket limits often carry higher premiums, so you pay more every month for that protection.


## How Deductibles and Out-of-Pocket Maximums Work with HSAs and FSAs


Tax-advantaged accounts like HSAs and FSAs help you pay for health care expenses with pre-tax dollars, and your deductible and out-of-pocket maximum are a practical guide to how much to put into them. Deductibles, copays, and coinsurance for medical care are qualified expenses for both accounts. (New to these accounts? Start with our comparison of[HSA vs. FSA](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-are-hsas-fsas) .)


High-deductible health plans usually have lower monthly premiums but higher deductibles and out-of-pocket maximums, and they're the plans that let you contribute to a Health Savings Account. For 2026,[IRS rules](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p969) require an HSA-qualified HDHP to have a minimum deductible of $1,700 (self-only) or $3,400 (family), with out-of-pocket maximums no higher than $8,500 and $17,000. Starting in 2026, bronze and catastrophic plans also count as HSA-compatible, under[IRS Notice 2026-5](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/n-26-05.pdf) ; see our[HSA eligibility expansion guide](https://www.withflex.com/blog/hsa-eligibility-expansion-2026) . If you're weighing a traditional plan against an HDHP, our[PPO vs. HDHP](https://www.withflex.com/blog/ppo-vs-hdhp) comparison walks through the trade-offs.


FSAs can also cover deductibles, copays, and coinsurance, but unused money is generally forfeited after the plan's deadline unless your plan offers a carryover (up to $680 of unused 2026 funds) or a grace period of up to two and a half months. Our guide to[FSA rollover rules](https://www.withflex.com/blog/use-or-lose-fsa-expire) explains the details, so estimate your spending carefully.


Here's a simple way to connect your plan limits to your contributions:


- **Start with your deductible.** If you expect to use care beyond preventive services, plan to cover at least that amount.
- **Add known expenses.** Physical therapy, a scheduled procedure, or ongoing prescriptions can push your spending past the deductible.
- **Consider your out-of-pocket maximum.** If you expect a high-cost year, estimate how close you might get to the cap and fund accordingly, within your account's annual limit.
- **Use last year as a baseline.** Review what you spent and adjust for anything new.


## A Year with a Deductible and Out-of-Pocket Maximum, Step by Step


To see how these limits work together, follow a year in the life of a hypothetical plan member.


**Meet Jordan.** Jordan has an employer plan with a $2,000 deductible, 20% coinsurance, and a $7,000 out-of-pocket maximum, and uses an HSA to pay for medical costs.


**Phase 1: Before the deductible (January–March).** In February, Jordan sees a specialist for a persistent knee issue. The visit costs $350 at the in-network negotiated rate, and Jordan pays the full $350 because the deductible hasn't been met. A preventive screening in March is covered at $0. Jordan pays the specialist bill from the HSA.


Running total toward the deductible: $350. Toward the out-of-pocket max: $350.


**Phase 2: After the deductible (April–July).** In April, Jordan needs an MRI ($1,200) and follow-up visits ($450). That brings Jordan's spending to $2,000, so the deductible is met. From here, the plan pays 80% of covered costs and Jordan pays 20% coinsurance. A $500 physical therapy series in June costs Jordan $100.


Running total toward the deductible: $2,000 (met). Toward the out-of-pocket max: $2,100.


**Phase 3: Reaching the out-of-pocket maximum (August–October).** In August, Jordan tears a knee ligament and needs surgery. The procedure and hospital stay total $28,000. Jordan's 20% coinsurance would be $5,600, but Jordan has already paid $2,100 toward a $7,000 cap, so Jordan owes only $4,900 more.


Running total toward the out-of-pocket max: $7,000 (met).


**Phase 4: After the out-of-pocket max (November–December).** Follow-up visits, more physical therapy, and prescriptions are covered at 100% for the rest of the plan year. Jordan pays $0 for covered in-network care.


What didn't count toward Jordan's limits: monthly premiums, a $200 out-of-network chiropractor visit, and a supplement the plan doesn't cover. Jordan paid for those, but they didn't move either threshold.


## Individual vs. Family Deductibles and Out-of-Pocket Maximums


Family plans add a layer of complexity because many use an "embedded" structure, where each family member has individual limits nested inside larger family limits.


**How embedded family deductibles work:**


- Each person has an individual deductible (say, $1,500).
- Everyone's spending also counts toward a family deductible (say, $3,000).
- If one person reaches their individual deductible, cost sharing starts for that person, even if the family deductible hasn't been met.
- If several family members' spending adds up to $3,000, the family deductible is met for everyone.


Some plans, including many HDHPs, use a non-embedded (aggregate) deductible instead, where the plan doesn't start sharing costs for anyone until the whole family deductible is met.


**How family out-of-pocket maximums work:**


- Each person has an individual out-of-pocket limit, which can't exceed $10,600 in 2026 on non-grandfathered plans.
- The family has a combined limit, up to $21,200 under ACA rules.
- When one person reaches their individual limit, their covered in-network care is paid in full, regardless of the family total.
- When the family's combined covered costs reach the family limit, remaining covered care is paid at 100% for everyone.


**Example:** The Garcias, two parents and two kids, have a plan with a $1,500 individual deductible, $3,000 family deductible, $8,000 individual out-of-pocket max, and $16,000 family limit. Their 8-year-old needs ongoing therapy and a minor surgery, adding up to large covered bills. Under the embedded design, the child reaches their individual deductible and then their individual out-of-pocket maximum, and the child's remaining covered care is paid in full, even though the rest of the family has barely used the plan.


Families expecting a baby, a child in ongoing therapy, or someone managing a chronic condition should look closely at both the individual and family out-of-pocket maximums, not just the deductible, because those caps set the true worst-case cost.


## How to Use These Limits When Comparing Plans in 2026


When you compare health insurance plans during open enrollment, the deductible and out-of-pocket maximum tell you more about your real costs than the premium alone. Our[open enrollment cheat sheet](https://www.withflex.com/blog/your-2026-open-enrollment-cheat-sheet-7-terms-you-actually-need-to-know) covers the other terms you'll see.


**ACA Marketplace tiers:**


- **Bronze plans** typically have the highest deductibles and out-of-pocket maximums but the lowest monthly premiums.
- **Silver plans** balance premiums and cost sharing, and if your income qualifies, cost-sharing reductions on a silver plan can lower your deductible and out-of-pocket maximum.
- **Gold plans** carry lower deductibles and out-of-pocket caps but higher premiums, which can suit people who expect regular medical care.


**Employer plans** often offer a traditional PPO alongside an HDHP. The HDHP usually has a higher deductible but lower premiums and HSA eligibility; the PPO may have a lower deductible but higher monthly premiums. Out-of-pocket maximums on employer plans vary by design, and many are set well below the federal limit.


**Guidance for three common situations:**


- **Generally healthy, low expected use:** A higher deductible with lower premiums may cost less overall, especially paired with HSA contributions. The higher out-of-pocket max is a risk, but a manageable one if you have savings set aside.
- **Known high use (chronic condition, planned surgery, pregnancy):** Prioritize a lower out-of-pocket maximum, even with higher premiums. You're likely to reach your deductible early, so the real question is your total cost for the year.
- **Families with unpredictable needs:** Look closely at embedded individual limits and the family out-of-pocket max. A plan with slightly higher premiums but a lower family limit can cost less in a year when one child needs unexpected care.


Always check both the deductible and the out-of-pocket maximum on the plan's Summary of Benefits and Coverage, not just the premium.


## Deductible or Out-of-Pocket Maximum: Which Should You Focus On?


- The deductible is the first cost threshold you'll face: it sets how much you pay before your insurance company starts sharing costs.
- The out-of-pocket maximum is your financial ceiling: the most you'll spend on covered in-network care in a plan year.
- Deductible payments count toward the out-of-pocket maximum, so they aren't separate expenses stacked on top of each other.
- Monthly premiums don't count toward either limit, but they move in the opposite direction from them.


**Focus more on the deductible if** you're in good health, rarely need care beyond preventive services, and want lower monthly premiums.


**Focus more on the out-of-pocket maximum if** you have a chronic condition, expect major medical bills (surgery, pregnancy, ongoing treatment), or want the strongest safety net against a costly year.


**Balance both if** you're a family with unpredictable needs, you plan to use an HSA or FSA, or you want to model both a typical year and an expensive one before you choose.


No single number tells the whole story, but knowing how your deductible and out-of-pocket maximum work together puts you in control of your health care costs.
